facts.text: The Australasian figbird is also known as the green figbird.
facts.quote: The Australasian figbird (Sphecotheres vieilloti), also known as the green figbird (not to be confused with the Timor figbird), is a conspicuous, medium-sized passerine bird

facts.text: The Australasian figbird is probably the largest of the Old World orioles, weighing around 111 to 130 g.
facts.quote: With a body mass of around 111 to 130 g (3.9 to 4.6 oz), it is probably the largest of the Old World orioles.

facts.text: Male Australasian figbirds have a black head, bright red facial skin, and a black bill with a red base.
facts.quote: Males of all subspecies have a black tail with broad white tips to the outer rectrices, white crissum (the undertail coverts surrounding the cloaca), blackish primaries, a black head, distinct bright red facial skin, a black bill with a red base, and pinkish legs.

facts.text: Female Australasian figbirds are drab, dull brownish above and white below with strong dark streaking.
facts.quote: Females are drab-coloured, being dull brownish above, and white below with strong dark streaking.

facts.text: The Australasian figbird can mimic the voices of other birds, such as parrots and other orioles.
facts.quote: Australasian figbirds make a large number of different short calls, and are also able to mimic the voices of other birds, for example parrots and other species of orioles.

facts.text: The Australasian figbird's song consists of a series of simple whistles.
facts.quote: The song consists of a series of simple whistles.

facts.text: Australasian figbirds eat mostly fruit, but also take small insects, nectar and small seeds.
facts.quote: As suggested by their name, Australasian figbirds are largely frugivorous, but also take small insects, nectar and small seeds.

facts.text: Unlike most orioles, Australasian figbirds are gregarious, forming flocks of 20 to 40 birds outside the breeding season.
facts.quote: Unlike most orioles, Australasian figbirds are gregarious, often forming flocks of 20 to 40 birds during the nonbreeding season, and even breeding in small, loose colonies.

facts.text: The Australasian figbird's clutch of two to four eggs is incubated by both sexes and hatches after 16–17 days.
facts.quote: The clutch of two to four eggs is incubated by both sexes, and typically hatches after 16–17 days.

facts.text: Australasian figbirds sometimes nest near spangled drongos and helmeted friarbirds, which may keep nest predators away.
facts.quote: It has been recorded nesting near the aggressive spangled drongo and helmeted friarbird, possibly gaining an advantage as they keep potential nest predators away.
